introduction: Mind, soul, spirit, heart, intellect: these readings, most of them from talks of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, use the words as several names for one life, lodged in a body it uses as an instrument and is not confined to. The older scriptures use the same handful of words just as freely, and the philosophers have argued for two thousand years over what the readings assume: that there is a rider as well as a horse. Their company here includes those who divide the person differently, those who think the mind begins empty, and Hume, who looked for the self and found only perceptions.
questions: Paul, the Katha Upanishad and Plato each divide the person into parts. Which division is nearest to that of the readings, and does it matter that the words differ?
The readings say that heart and mind are one, and also that the intellect should become the servant of the heart. How do Pascal and Hume help in reading the two statements together?
Simmias in the Phaedo compares the soul to the harmony of a lyre, which ends with the instrument. What do the readings on fever, sleep and the rider answer?
Proverbs, Juvenal and Shakespeare all link the state of the body with the state of the mind. Where do the readings agree, and where do they set a limit?
Hume could never catch himself without a perception. What would the reading that says “show me what it is that thinks in me” ask him next?

outside.why: The talk speaks of body, soul and spirit, with the soul between. Paul’s blessing names the same three: your whole spirit and soul and body.

Intelligence is “the intermediary between his body and his spirit”. Pope describes the creature who lives in that middle: placed on this isthmus of a middle state, a being darkly wise and rudely great.
“The mind therefore has no place.” The Book of Job asks for its address and finds none: where shall wisdom be found, and where is the place of understanding?
The spirit is the lamp and the mind the light that shines from it. Elihu in Job: there is a spirit in man, and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding.
Mind, soul and spirit are names for one sign in man. The great commandment uses three such names for one act of love: with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.
Spirit, mind and soul each have their office. The Katha Upanishad gives the offices to a chariot: the Self sits in it, the body is the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins.
“At death everything but Spirit is destroyed.” The Preacher: then shall the dust return to the earth as it was.
Among the parts of the body “both spiritual and physical connections are clear”. Paul makes a parable of it: if the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing?

“It is the same agency functioning in different degrees.” Faust does not feel like one agency: two souls, alas, reside within my breast, and each withdraws from its brother. Is the division he feels a difference of degrees, or something the reading leaves out?

Heart and mind, the answer says, “are one”. Pascal’s most quoted sentence keeps them apart: the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know. Is he speaking of the two kinds of mind the answer goes on to name?
Intellect and heart “are one”, named by their use. Proverbs has the heart do the mind’s work without remark: as he thinketh in his heart, so is he.
The intellect “develops and weakens” while the soul stays the same. Paul says it of age and hardship: though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
The mind force directs the members, each with “its own special function”. Paul turns the same picture toward a community: many members in one body, and all members have not the same office.
The mirror for divine reflection “is the whole body”. Paul gives the body a like dignity in another figure: your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you.

Intelligence “does not partake of the quality of space”. Dickinson measures it against space and finds it the larger: the brain is wider than the sky, for put them side by side, the one the other will include.
“Reason is a monarch over the body and the five senses.” Plato’s monarch has trouble with his team: one horse noble, the other ignoble, and the driving of them gives a great deal of trouble.
Hume turned the throne over: reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions. Is he denying that reason governs, or describing what happens when it tries to govern alone?
Thought and consciousness have their seat in the brain, and the heart has its part. The Dhammapada begins with how far thought reaches: all that we are is the result of what we have thought.
“The members are instruments and the spirit is the doer.” Marcus Aurelius quotes Epictetus more bleakly: thou art a little soul bearing about a corpse. Is an instrument the same thing as a burden?
The reading counts the powers of perception, outward and inward. Hamlet runs through them in wonder: how noble in reason, how infinite in faculty, in apprehension how like a god.
The faculties must be gathered “that man may be perfected”. Aristotle names the one that makes the gathering human: reason more than anything else is man.
“The eye is the means for the transmission of light to the mind.” Jesus uses the eye the same way: the light of the body is the eye, and if thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
Deafness, the talk says, is the greater hindrance, since understanding comes by the ear. Paul’s sentence gives hearing the same place: faith cometh by hearing.
The body is “purely animal in type”; something else thinks. Genesis tells it in two acts: man formed of the dust of the ground, and the breath of life breathed into him.

The Preacher looks at the same animal body and stops there: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; they have all one breath; a man hath no preeminence above a beast. What does the reading see that he, in this mood, does not?
“The thought force and the animal force are partners.” Jesus in Gethsemane on how unequal the partners can be: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
The human spirit “encompasses all things”. Pascal: by space the universe encompasses and swallows me up like an atom; by thought I comprehend the world.
The mind “frees man from the fetters” and leads him on. Paul expects the change to come by the same road: be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.

A faculty in man frees him “from all the fetters of self”. Milton gives the mind that power, in the mouth of Satan, who uses it to stay as he is: the mind is its own place, and in itself can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.

The perceiving soul “discovers” what was veiled. Locke supposed the mind to be white paper, void of all characters, and all its materials to come from experience. Can a blank page discover, or must the discoverer bring something of its own?

Every creature apprehends “sensible realities”; the intelligible are disclosed only to the knower. Wordsworth’s Peter Bell has only the first: a primrose by a river’s brim a yellow primrose was to him, and it was nothing more.
The “light of Intuition” comprehends the core of things. Emerson asks a man to watch for it: that gleam of light which flashes across his mind from within.
Locke would not let an inner light sit above examination: reason must be our last judge and guide in every thing. How is an intuition to be told from a strong wish without the judge he names?

No criterion is perfect, since “the mind itself is liable to error”. Descartes, knowing it, made a rule instead of giving up: never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such. Does a careful method answer the reading’s doubt, or only reduce it?
“The light of the intellect” is manifestor and seer. Aristotle chose the same figure for the mind that acts: a sort of positive state like light, which makes potential colours into actual colours.
The spiritual power “perceives essential realities”, unseen and without shape. Paul: the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
Man has “two kinds of sight”. Wordsworth, lying on his couch, has the daffodils flash upon that inward eye which is the bliss of solitude.
The spirit acts without instruments “in the world of dreams”. The Qur’an sets sleep beside death: God receiveth souls at the time of their death, and that which dieth not yet in its sleep.

In sleep the spirit “soars to loftier heights”. Mercutio has the common opinion of dreams: the children of an idle brain, begot of nothing but vain fantasy. What kind of dream would be needed to show him wrong?
Things enter the mind which “afterwards become manifest in outward form”. Joseph’s dream of the sheaves is the scriptural case, told to brothers who hated him the more for it.
Not to fight evil thoughts but to turn elsewhere. Paul’s counsel is to fill the mind: whatsoever things are true, honest, just, pure, lovely.

One should not “try to control them, for this is impossible”. Paul elsewhere speaks of bringing into captivity every thought. Are the two counsels opposed, or is his captivity the turning that the answer recommends?
“Be not the slave of your moods, but their master.” Proverbs ranks that mastery above conquest: he that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city.
Good news may “entirely dispel the ailment”. Proverbs knew the effect in both directions: a merry heart doeth good like a medicine, but a broken spirit drieth the bones.

The nerve stands “between the two systems”, and health needs both in order. Macbeth asks the doctor to minister to a mind diseased and is told that therein the patient must minister to himself. Where does the physician’s work end, by the reading’s account?
“The more the body is healthful the greater will be the power of the spirit.” Juvenal’s line is the proverb for it: you should pray for a sound mind in a sound body.
Starving the body for the mind’s sake “is imagination”. Nerissa in The Merchant of Venice: they are as sick that surfeit with too much as they that starve with nothing.

Fever is “a defect in the instrument”, not in the spirit. Simmias puts the objection to Socrates: harmony too is invisible and divine, abiding in the lyre, yet it does not outlast the strings. What in the readings answers him?
It is “the soul which feels the pain”. Proverbs makes the same point from the other side: the spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity, but a wounded spirit who can bear?
“Sometimes the rider moves without a mount.” Jesus sends out the twelve with that confidence: fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.
The atheist is asked to show “what it is that thinks in me”. Hamlet to his sceptical friend: there are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy.

Hume took up the challenge and looked: when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception; I never can catch myself. Does his failure to find the thinker count for the atheist, or for the reading?
The waves of the mind “never stop for one instant”. Shakespeare hears in the waves the minutes of a life: each changing place with that which goes before, in sequent toil all forwards do contend.
The intellect is of little avail until it is “the servant of the heart”. Pascal gives the reason he would offer: it is the heart which experiences God, and not the reason.

Soul, mind and spirit have been interchanged, but there are “three aspects of our humanness”. Dr Jekyll counted differently: man is not truly one, but truly two. Does it matter how many parts are counted, if the person is one?
Mind and Kingdom alike have “no place”. Jesus, asked when the kingdom should come: neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for the kingdom of God is within you.
